title: The Cascade - Specificity and Inheritance
summary: Explains how the browser resolves conflicting CSS rules through four ranked categories: position, specificity, type and importance. Includes three quick quiz questions and an exercise that recolours nested boxes using only CSS, with no HTML changes.

concepts.heading: What the cascade is
points: The cascade only matters when several rules target the same element and set the same property. The browser must decide which declaration wins; the rest are ignored.
Every matching rule is applied in turn, so a later or stronger one overwrites an earlier one. What the user sees is the result left at the end.

Worked example: li { color: green } in the external stylesheet turns an ordered list green; adding style="color: red" to one li makes just that item red, because inline styles come last in the process.
Four categories decide the winner, listed from weakest to strongest: position, specificity, type, importance. Inside each category there is a smaller ranking of its own.

concepts.heading: 1. Position
points: When two declarations are equal in every other respect, the one written lower in the file wins.
This applies inside one rule block (setting color twice, the second sticks) and across rules (a second li selector further down overrides the first).
It holds in both external stylesheets and internal <style> blocks.

concepts.heading: 2. Specificity
points: Specificity measures how narrowly a selector aims at an element. Take an li with id="first-id", class="first-class" and the draggable attribute: four different selectors can all hit it.
Ranking from least to most specific as taught: element selector (li), class selector (.first-class), attribute selector (li[draggable]), id selector (#first-id).
An id is the strongest because a page should hold only one element with a given id, so it points to a single element. A class can be shared by many elements.

The lecture ranks attribute above class because in practice it overrode the class in her demo. (Extra) The official specificity rules give class, attribute and pseudo-class selectors the same weight, so ties between them fall back to position. Do not rely on attribute beating class.

(Extra) A common mental scoring is inline 1000, id 100, class/attribute 10, element 1, and the highest total wins. Selectors are really compared column by column rather than added in base 10, but the model is fine for everyday use.
If all four selectors were written and each set a different colour, the most specific one (the id rule, orange in her example) is what the page shows.

concepts.heading: 3. Type (where the CSS lives)
points: External stylesheet via <link>, internal CSS in a <style> element, and inline CSS in a style attribute.
Strength order: inline beats internal, which beats external.
Reasoning: inline targets a single element, internal covers one page, external may be shared by many pages.
The browser conceptually checks external first, then internal, then inline, with each later layer overwriting the previous.

concepts.heading: 4. Importance (!important)
points: Add !important after the value, before the semicolon, to make that declaration beat position, specificity and type.
It overrides even an inline style or an id selector, and works wherever the rule sits in the file.
(Extra) Use it sparingly: once several rules carry it, you are back to fighting over order and specificity, and debugging gets harder.

concepts.heading: Using the cascade as a debugging checklist
points: When a style is not showing, walk the categories from the top: is something marked !important, is an inline style overriding, is a more specific selector winning, is a later rule overriding?
Treat the summary diagram as a reference to keep beside you rather than something to memorise.

concepts.heading: Quiz answers (worked through)
points: Quiz 1: an h1 with a class and an id, two external rules, one by class (blue) and one by id (green). Specificity decides, the id wins, result green.
Quiz 2: an h1 with two classes (an element can carry several, separated by spaces), and two class rules of equal specificity. Position decides, the lower rule wins, result blue.
Quiz 3: an h1 with an id rule in CSS and also an inline style. Type outranks specificity, so inline wins, result blue.
Lesson from quiz 3: a rule that wins in one category can still lose to a higher-ranked category, so keep the order of the big categories in mind.

task.name: 7.1 CSS Cascade: recolour the nested boxes
task.starting_point: index.html has an outer div with id outer-box and class box, which contains two div.box wrappers, each holding a yellow paragraph and an inner div with classes box and inner-box that holds a paragraph with class white-text. style.css already has rules for .box (blue background, 10px padding) and p (yellow, no margin or padding). HTML and existing CSS must stay unchanged.
task.goal: Match the goal image: white text in the innermost paragraphs, red inner boxes, and a purple outer box, with 10px padding on every box.
steps: Add a rule for .white-text setting color to white.
Add a rule for .inner-box setting background-color to red. Place it below the .box rule, otherwise the later .box rule overrides it.
Add a rule for #outer-box setting background-color to purple. The id is the only thing that distinguishes this div from the other .box divs.
Do not add padding: all three boxes already share the class box, which provides the 10px.
Compare the preview with the goal image.
task.expected_result: Purple outer container, blue middle boxes, red inner boxes; yellow text in the middle boxes, white text in the red ones.

pitfalls: Putting .inner-box above .box: both are class selectors, so the later .box blue overrides red.
Expecting a p rule to beat .white-text just because p is written lower. Here .white-text is more specific than the element selector p, so it wins wherever it sits.
Adding extra padding to #outer-box changes the result, because the id rule outranks .box.
Overusing !important to force styles instead of fixing selector order or specificity.
Assuming specificity outranks everything: inline styles beat id selectors.

playground.coverage: Tasks and starter/solution files match the course exercise. Explore demos cover specificity scores with toggles (including !important) and an order-matters demo. Notes list the four weights and mention DevTools strikethroughs.
gaps_and_ideas: The playground's weight order lists position, specificity, type, importance, which matches. Add a type demo showing external vs internal vs inline on one heading.
Add the three quizzes as a self-check widget (pick blue or green, reveal the reason).
Note the course ranks attribute above class; the playground scoring treats them as equal at 10, which is the spec-correct version. Add a short callout explaining the difference.
Add a task about multiple classes on one element (class="a-class another-class") and the position tie-break.
Task 3 hints about moving .white-text above p; clarify that it still works because class beats element, to avoid confusing it with the .inner-box ordering case.
